connections.label: Cecilia Levy
connections.note: Levy's faculty page lists 'Szydagis, Knight, Levy, The Snowball chamber: neutron induced nucleation in supercooled water' (arXiv:1807.09253, 2018) and describes the Snowball Chamber as 'a research topic completely unique to the UAlbany dark matter group'. The UAlbany release makes the methodological carry-over explicit: the C-TAP frame-differencing software is 'similar to an approach used by physicists like him and Levy to look for direct evidence of dark matter'. This is the mechanism by which rare-event detection practice reached UAP field work at this institution.

connections.label: University at Albany (SUNY), Department of Physics
connections.note: The department's own faculty page for Szydagis lists his research interests as 'Experimental astroparticle physics, in particular direct detection of dark matter WIMPs (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles) and general detector development for rare event searches, neutron activation, and Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena'. That the phrase appears on a university department page, not a personal site, is the load-bearing fact: UAP is here a declared institutional research interest rather than a private hobby. Szydagis created the Noble Element Simulation Technique (NEST) in 2011 and works on LZ at the Sanford Underground Research Facility.

label: Matthew Szydagis
narrative: Szydagis is the instrumentation conscience of the field. His day job is liquid-xenon dark-matter detection - he is a principal author of the Noble Element Simulation Technique (NEST) and has published on xenon bubble chambers and low-energy nuclear recoils - which means his professional standard for what counts as a detection is set by an experiment that has spent decades not finding something. He carried that standard into UAP work by co-founding UAPx with Kevin Knuth and running an instrumented field campaign off Catalina Island, publishing 'Initial results from the first field expedition of UAPx to study unidentified anomalous phenomena' in Progress in Aerospace Sciences 156:101099 in June 2025 with Knuth, Benjamin Kugielsky and Cecilia Levy. That paper matters less for what it found than for what it establishes: a multi-instrument, multi-band, published protocol with stated false-positive handling, in a mainstream aerospace journal, done by people who build particle detectors. He also published in Limina, the journal of UAP studies, in March 2025 on disclosure timelines. In June 2026 he was named to the UAP Science Advisory Council in the instrumentation and data-collection role, which puts a working detector physicist on the government's outside science body.
